title: Hierarchical sensory processing in zebrafish thalamocortical-like circuits.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Found the data DOI in the authors' GitHub README (github.com/yaksilab/PG-Pallium_paper), resolved it through DataCite to the NIRD Research Data Archive page, and downloaded the archive's own table-of-contents and summary CSVs plus its RO-Crate metadata (licence CC-BY-4.0). Confirmed with an HTTP HEAD that the single deposited file, CollectedData_Trinh_et_al_2026.7z, is public (HTTP 200, no login) and is 21,002,892,983 bytes (21.0 GB). Then read the 7-Zip archive's internal headers with two ranged HTTP requests (32 bytes at the start, 430 KB at the end) and decoded them with py7zr: 37 entries, 31 MATLAB .mat files in 6 folders plus one ReadMe .docx, 21.6 GB uncompressed, in large solid compression blocks (one block alone is 8.4 GB).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All biology and sample sizes come from the bioRxiv preprint of the same study (10.1101/2025.09.15.675867), because the Science article is paywalled and absent from PubMed Central: two-photon calcium imaging of preglomerular complex (PG) neurons in 11 fish, PG axons in the pallium in 12 fish, pallial neurons in 10 fish, with light (visual) and tap (mechano-vibrational) stimuli. Neuron counts, trial counts, the contents and column names of any .mat file, the units of the activity values, and the coordinate system were never seen - only the file names and byte sizes.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified in the repository, not just the paper: the NIRD Research Data Archive deposit is public under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0, and a HEAD request on the download link returns HTTP 200 with no login or application.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: NOT VERIFIED - read from file names only. Small '*_Analysis.mat' and '*Kmeans*.mat' files (64 KB to 1.3 MB) almost certainly hold per-neuron response amplitudes, selectivity and cluster labels, but I could not open them, so whether the target is a ready column is unconfirmed.

a3_inputs_present.note: NOT VERIFIED beyond file names. The large '*_Data.mat' files (0.5-6 GB) should contain the activity traces themselves and the '*SpatialCorr*' / '*Focality*' files should contain neuron coordinates, so inputs look present rather than referenced elsewhere.

a4_units_stated.note: NOT VERIFIED. A ReadMe_Dataset_Trinh2026.docx (64 KB) ships with the data and presumably documents units, but it sits at the end of the last solid compression block and is unreachable without the whole 21 GB. Calcium imaging is conventionally reported as unitless relative fluorescence change.

a5_enough_rows.note: NOT VERIFIED. No neuron count was seen anywhere. The paper reports 10-12 fish per imaging dataset, so the independent unit is roughly a dozen animals even if the neuron rows number in the thousands.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 21.0 GB download, 21.6 GB uncompressed, ~43 GB transient disk; individual .mat files up to 6.05 GB
a6_fits_laptop.note: KILLER, verified from the archive's own headers. The entire deposit is one 21.0 GB 7-Zip file holding 21.6 GB of MATLAB files, and the compression is solid, so the small per-neuron summary tables cannot be pulled out without streaming through multi-gigabyte blocks. There is no subsetting or streaming route to a small working set, the single biggest .mat file is 6.05 GB on its own, and the project's own rule caps downloads at 50 MB with a 5 GB working set.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Only the coarse structure could be checked, and it matches: folders for PG neurons, PG axons, in vivo and ex vivo pallial neurons, and simultaneous PG-plus-pallium recordings, exactly the experiment set described in the preprint. No row count was comparable.

a8_label_provenance.note: NOT VERIFIED, and a real concern. Response classes come from the authors' own thresholding of calcium traces, which is fine, but the files named 'Kmeans' mean the published functional categories are unsupervised-clustering output, and 'PGNeurons_SVM_PositionsResults.mat' (483 MB) shows a support vector machine decoder was already fitted, so some candidate labels are model outputs rather than measurements.

existing_models.name: ZAPBench (Zebrafish Activity Prediction Benchmark), Google Research and HHMI Janelia, ICLR 2025
existing_models.score_and_split: Public benchmark for forecasting cellular-resolution activity of over 70,000 neurons in one larval zebrafish brain, with held-out future time windows and several published baselines (linear, time-series and video models); code and data are open at github.com/google-research/zapbench.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Their reported weak spot is exactly the region this paper studies: the dorsal-anterior pallium is the hardest area to predict, being driven by learning and memory rather than immediate sensory input.

existing_models.name: The paper's own support vector machine position decoder (file 202606_PGNeurons_SVM_PositionsResults.mat, 483 MB)
existing_models.score_and_split: Its existence is inferred from the archive file listing and the MATLAB analysis code in the authors' GitHub repository; no score or split could be read because the file is inside the 21 GB archive.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not determined - the published discussion was not accessible (the Science article is paywalled and not in PubMed Central).

backbone.name: None appropriate. Single-cell transcriptome backbones (scGPT, Geneformer) do not take calcium traces, and there is no open pretrained model for zebrafish pallial activity; ZAPBench baselines are task-specific time-series models, not freeze-and-head backbones.

integration.partner_dataset: ZAPBench / the mapzebrain reference brain atlas, joinable in principle by registering neuron coordinates into a common zebrafish brain template
integration.join_key: 3D anatomical coordinates in a shared reference brain, which would first have to be built - the deposit's coordinate frame is unknown and the fish are juveniles (21-28 days) while ZAPBench uses 6-day larvae
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the functional hierarchies found in the juvenile pallium appear in independent whole-brain larval recordings at the same anatomical locations? - a good question, but the age mismatch and the missing registration make the join speculative rather than available.

controls.positive_control: Would be available in principle: the model must recover the paper's headline topography, namely that visual-specific responses sit in one pallial zone and vibration-specific ones in another, and that multimodal and coincidence-detecting neurons concentrate at the boundary.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling and distance shuffling, both already implemented in the authors' MATLAB code, so a fair comparison exists.
controls.external_validation: A goldfish pallium sensory mapping paper (Brain Structure & Function 2026, voltage-sensitive dye imaging of modality-specific pallial domains) is a genuinely independent second source, but it measures a different signal in a different species with no shared identifiers.

honest_claim_h3: Using 10-12 juvenile zebrafish per condition from a single laboratory, a model could claim at most that a neuron's position within the pallium predicts whether that neuron is visual-specific, vibration-specific or multimodal, in animals of this age, prepared and imaged by this one lab.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a brain cell's position in the zebrafish forebrain to predict which senses it responds to and how it combines them.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one neuron: its three-dimensional position in the pallium (the fish's cortex-like forebrain region) and, optionally, its activity trace. Number of neurons unknown - never verified; the paper reports only 10-12 fish per imaging dataset.
plain_idea.predict: The neuron's functional class - responds only to light, only to vibration, to both, or shows a non-additive 'coincidence detector' response. The true answer comes from two-photon calcium imaging, which measures a fluorescence change when a neuron becomes active.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Comparative neuroscientists arguing about whether the fish forebrain is organised like the mammalian cortex would get a quantitative map instead of qualitative pictures. Even a failure would show how much functional identity is not predictable from location.

more_or_better_data.why: ZAPBench holds over 70,000 neurons from a whole brain with open, chunk-accessible files; this deposit covers 10-12 juvenile fish per condition in one 21 GB blob whose neuron count I could not even read.

confidence_score.why: The design does support honest uncertainty - responses are measured over repeated stimulus trials and across 10-12 animals, so per-neuron reliability and between-fish spread are computable, and the authors' own code already computes trial-to-trial cluster fidelity.

models_beatable.why: The paper's internal support vector machine decoder is a classical, pre-deep-learning method and would be easy to beat, but ZAPBench (2025) is current, open and honestly evaluated on held-out future time, and is not.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on nearly every condition: the baseline cannot be run (the paper's decoder is locked inside the archive), the assays differ (two-photon in juveniles versus light-sheet in larvae), and no shared evaluation split or coordinate frame exists.

ml_idea: Predict each pallial neuron's sensory response class (visual-only, vibration-only, multimodal, or non-additive coincidence detector) from its anatomical position, with leave-one-fish-out cross-validation, and test whether position-based prediction transfers from the preglomerular input layer to the pallial output layer. Attractive on paper, but the data is a single 21 GB solid archive with no route to the small summary tables, and the obvious labels are unsupervised cluster assignments rather than direct measurements.

effort.compute_note: Sizes are exact, read from the archive's own headers (21,002,892,983 bytes packed, 21.6 GB unpacked, largest single file 6.05 GB). The hours and RAM figures are estimates for downloading, extracting on roughly 43 GB of free disk, and loading one multi-gigabyte MATLAB file; nothing was timed because nothing could be opened.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already done, and it killed the project: read the deposit's table-of-contents CSV. It shows one file of 21.0 GB, so there is no small-file route in.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A6 on verified evidence. The whole deposit is a single public 21.0 GB 7-Zip archive (21.6 GB of MATLAB files, largest 6.05 GB) in solid compression blocks up to 8.4 GB, so the small per-neuron summary tables cannot be extracted without downloading everything - far past the 50 MB download and 5 GB working-set limits, with no streaming or subsetting route. Because nothing could be opened, A2, A4, A5 and A8 all stay unverified, and the two A8 warning signs are visible in the file names alone: the functional categories come from k-means clustering and a support vector machine was already fitted. The biology is first-rate and the licence is permissive, so if the authors ever post the small '*_Analysis.mat' files separately this becomes worth a second look; today it is unopenable on a laptop.
